stem: Wells’s central claim in this passage is that lynching in the South was primarily

options.text: a lawful punishment ordered by Southern courts
a response to crimes that Black men had actually committed
a form of terror meant to control Black Southerners
a practice that white Southerners had already abandoned by 1892

rationales.A: Wells describes mobs hanging and shooting men, not courts ordering punishment.
rationales.B: Wells calls the rape charge a lie nobody believes.
rationales.C: Wells counts eight lynchings in a single week and calls the rape charge “the old thread-bare lie.” Background: her pamphlet argues that lynching was not punishment for crime but a weapon to suppress Black political power and reassert white supremacy.
rationales.D: Eight lynchings in one week show the practice was active, not abandoned.
rationales.general:
1. Count what Wells reports. Eight lynchings in a single week.
2. Hear her judgment on the excuse. The rape charge is “the old thread-bare lie.”
3. Ask what is left when the excuse falls. Not lawful punishment and not a response to real crimes.
4. Match the claim. Background: Wells argued lynching was terror to control Black Southerners and reassert white supremacy.
Remember: when a writer knocks down the excuse for a practice, ask what purpose is left standing.

stimulus.source_note: Ida B. Wells, Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases (1892), quoting her editorial in the Memphis Free Speech, May 21, 1892. Public domain.
stimulus.text: “Eight negroes lynched since last issue of the Free Speech, one at Little Rock, Ark., . . . and five on the same old racket — the new alarm about raping white women. The same programme of hanging, then shooting bullets into the lifeless bodies was carried out to the letter. Nobody in this section of the country believes the old thread-bare lie that Negro men rape white women.”

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain pamphlet

primary_sources: Ida B. Wells, Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases (1892)
